Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Places of worship or religious gatherings

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette: Three years ago, Kiana was deployed to a makeshift aid depot on the outskirts of a conflict zone. When the artillery struck, the tent walls tore open, spilling her into a chaotic evacuation. Amidst the dust, a frantic medic pressed close to steady her, his heavy cologne mixing with the acrid smoke. When a supply runner made a sudden, sharp motion to direct them, Kiana's body went rigid, her instincts overriding her training. She was forced to leave a wounded local in the rubble to reach the extraction point, a split-second survival calculus that shattered her identity as a healer. In the aftermath, she could not reconstruct the event; some moments burned with terrifying precision while the hours surrounding them slipped into a blank void. When she tried to recount it to anyone, she invariably lost the thread. Within weeks, those olfactory cues and sudden shifts in posture began to dictate her survival strategy. The moment a familiar cologne drifted through a grocery aisle, the fragmented memory of the clinic surged forward, pulling her back into the chaos. That jarring recall immediately cemented her conviction that she had violated her deepest values and therefore belonged nowhere in the civilian world. Because she felt fundamentally broken, she instinctively turned to avoidance, steering clear of medical centers and religious gatherings where she felt unworthy of healing or sanctuary. Her husband's attempts at physical affection only amplified the danger; the very contact she once craved now felt like an invasion, tightening the knot of her self-reproach. She began to believe that any attempt to process the event would only unravel her further, so she let the silence harden into a wall. Over the following months, her internal alarm system recalibrated, turning ordinary life into a minefield. The persistent sense that she was fundamentally broken made the environment feel perpetually hostile, which in turn made her more vulnerable to the smell of cologne or a casual hug. This escalating threat monitoring dictated her avoidance; she refused to drive to unfamiliar trailheads, convinced that navigating unknown terrain would leave her powerless if violence erupted again. When she did patrol the national forest as a park ranger, every rustling branch or sudden gesture by a fellow ranger set her nervous system on high alert, which in turn activated her deepest triggers. Her constant scanning for danger fractured her recall, making it impossible to weave the partial flashes into a continuous timeline. She stopped seeking counseling, telling herself that psychological help offered no solace for what she had done, and this continued withdrawal ensured the traumatic fragments never integrated, leaving them sharp and ready to cut. Now thirty-nine, married to David, Kiana finds herself trapped in a tightening loop. Her refusal to seek help ensures her nervous system remains raw, meaning every cologne or sudden movement bypasses her coping mechanisms and strikes directly. Her avoidance of community spaces keeps her disconnected from those who might anchor her, reinforcing the belief that she belongs nowhere. Her conviction that her life has lost its value ensures she never sits down to piece together the fragmented moments, leaving the narrative permanently disjointed. She finally called the veteran assistance line not because she wants to talk, but because the weight of her own guilt has become heavier than her fear of the past. What she hopes for, quietly, is a way to lay down the guard she has carried for so long, even if it means remembering everything.
